name: Camsá
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Howard, Linda 1967/1972, Camsa phonology (SIL, Phonemic Systems of Colombian Languages); also O'Brien 2018 Kamsa grammatical description

new_statements.quote: Kamsá words generally have penultimate stress, although there are a few cases where stress is ultimate. Thus, stress is phonemic, not fully predictable. Stress cannot fall on syllables other than the penult or ultima. Some words have lexically determined ultimate stress. This is particularly common for nouns ending in /-a/, such as wabowán 'horrible' and batá 'aunt'. ... Words that end with closed syllables have penultimate stress. ... While ultimate stress can be lexically determined, it can be morphologically determined as well: verbs have ultimate stress in the infinitive ... (note that the infinitive always ends in -an).
new_statements.citation: O'Brien, Colleen Alena. 2018. A grammatical description of Kamsá, a language isolate of Colombia. PhD dissertation, University of Hawai'i at Mānoa.
new_statements.locator: Chapter 2 Phonology, section 2.4 'Stress', pp.46-47 (PDF pp.59-60); orthography note p.33
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Files checked in (1) 278 PDF pp., Word-generated text layer; title page 'A grammatical description of Kamsá, a language isolate of Colombia', Colleen Alena O'Brien, UH Mānoa, Dec 2018, committee chaired by Lyle Campbell). extracted text of PDF pp.59-60 = printed pp.46-47, section '2.4 Stress': the quoted sentences are all present verbatim in order; the three ellipses mark real omissions (the tendency remark on nouns in open -a/-o or closed -an; the /a o e/-only remark with batá/bakó/ʃaxbé and bastok/benach; and ', as in the following examples' before the parenthesis). Only difference is curly vs straight quotation marks. Surrounding text also confirms the reader's paraphrase: /i u ɨ/ never…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default word stress is on the penultimate syllable; a lexically marked minority of words (mostly nouns ending in open -a/-o or in -an) and verb infinitives in -án carry final stress; stress never falls earlier than the penult (two-syllable final window), final /i u ɨ/ are never stressed, and words ending in a closed syllable (other than -an) take penult stress. Howard 1967 (p.80) independently states the same: one phonemic stress per word, penultimate or final, penult most frequent, so only final stress is written; Spanish loans with antepenult stress are repaired to penult (numéro, muséca).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Neither O'Brien 2018 nor Howard 1967 mentions secondary stress. Howard 6.1 notes pitch follows primary stress (final-stressed words level; penult-stressed words drop on the final syllable; initial syllable of 4+-syllable words somewhat higher).
new_statements.exceptions: Lexical final stress (batá 'aunt', bakó 'uncle', ʃaxbé 'cucumber', wabowán 'horrible'); verb infinitives in -án (xaxanán 'to say'); minimal pair ena 'pure' (penult) vs ená 'seller' (final); stressed clitic té 'day' (kada-té 'each day', from Sp. día); final stressed /á/ resists the optional final-vowel deletion that other words undergo; Howard: penult-stressed words may devoice or drop the final vowel in connected speech.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level phonemic stress stated on citation forms; O'Brien's practical orthography (used throughout the grammar and by the community) writes an acute only on final-stressed words, unmarked = penult. Howard's analysis is of the phonological word; her pitch remarks (6.1) are word-level, 'not fully analyzed'.
new_statements.identity_note: Both sources describe the single Camsá/Kamsá speech community of the Sibundoy valley (Putumayo, Colombia), glottocode cams1241, ISO kbh; Howard spells it Camsá, O'Brien Kamsá (community spelling Kamëntšá). No dialect split is reported.

sources.locator: Chapter 2 Phonology, section 2.4 'Stress', pp.46-47 (PDF pp.59-60); orthography note p.33
sources.note: Ch.2 sec. 2.4 'Stress' pp.46-47: words generally have penultimate stress; a few have lexically (nouns in -a/-o/-an, e.g. batá 'aunt', bakó 'uncle') or morphologically (verb infinitives in -án) determined final stress; stress never falls earlier than the penult; final /i u ɨ/ never stressed; closed final syllables -> penult; minimal pair ena 'pure' vs ená 'seller'; clitic té 'day' always stressed; orthography marks only final stress (p.33).

sources.citation: Howard, Linda. 1967. Camsa phonology. In Viola G. Waterhouse (ed.), Phonemic systems of Colombian languages (SIL Publications in Linguistics and Related Fields 14), 73-87. Norman: Summer Institute of Linguistics of the University of Oklahoma.
sources.note: Sec. 4.1 'Stress' p.80: every word has one phonemic strong stress, on either the penultimate or the final syllable (canyá 'alone' vs cánye 'one', batá 'aunt', wáta 'year', bebínco vs bebincuá); penult is most frequent so only final stress is written. 6.1 p.84: pitch determined by stress placement. 6.2: stressed vowel slightly lengthened. 7 p.86: Spanish loans with stress 'too far forward' move it to the penult (numéro < número, muséca < música, lastéma < lástima).
